lab_title: Unveiling Molecular Shapes: An AR Exploration of VSEPR Theory
top_level_objectives: Understand the fundamental principles of VSEPR theory.
Identify electron domains around a central atom in a Lewis structure.
Predict the electron-domain geometry based on the number of electron domains.
Predict the molecular geometry, considering the influence of lone pairs.
Explain the role of lone pairs in distorting idealized bond angles.
Relate VSEPR predictions to the observed shapes of common molecules.

scenes.brief_purpose: Lay the groundwork for VSEPR by defining electron domains and demonstrating the principle of minimizing electron-pair repulsion.
key_visuals: A holographic representation of a generic central atom.
Interactive virtual 'electron domains' that can be added and moved, showing repulsion and rearrangement.
student_actions: Add one electron domain, then a second, observing how they naturally move to opposite sides.
Add a third and fourth, seeing them settle into trigonal planar and tetrahedral arrangements.

scenes.brief_purpose: Systematically explore and identify the linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: Interactive models showing a central atom with 2, 3, and 4 electron domains.
Highlighting the resulting geometric shapes and bond angles.
student_actions: Construct each geometry (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral) by adding the correct number of electron domains.
Confirm the geometry name and ideal bond angles.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the more complex trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: Interactive models showing a central atom with 5 and 6 electron domains.
Demonstrating the distinct axial/equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal and the uniform positions in octahedral.
student_actions: Assemble the trigonal bipyramidal geometry with 5 electron domains, noting the two types of positions.
Then, assemble the octahedral geometry with 6 electron domains.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain how lone pairs modify electron-domain geometry to produce molecular geometry, focusing on systems with up to 4 electron domains.
key_visuals: An interface to convert a bonding pair to a lone pair.
Visualizations of water (bent) and ammonia (trigonal pyramidal) with their Lewis structures.
student_actions: Start with a tetrahedral electron domain.
Convert one bonding pair to a lone pair to see trigonal pyramidal, then another to see bent.
Compare these AR models with displayed real molecules like ammonia and water.

scenes.scene_name: Advanced Molecular Geometries with Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the concept of lone pair influence to systems with 5 and 6 electron domains, illustrating more complex molecular shapes.
key_visuals: Interactive models of trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain structures.
Options to convert bonding pairs to lone pairs, showing shapes like seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, and square pyramidal.
student_actions: Experiment with converting bonding pairs to lone pairs in the trigonal bipyramidal structure to form seesaw and T-shaped geometries.
Then, do the same for the octahedral structure to form square planar and square pyramidal shapes.

scenes.scene_name: The Repulsive Power of Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: Investigate why lone pairs exert greater repulsion, leading to deviations from ideal bond angles.
key_visuals: Side-by-side AR models of methane, ammonia, and water, with their experimentally observed bond angles highlighted.
A visual representation emphasizing the larger spatial requirement of a lone pair compared to a bonding pair.
student_actions: Compare the C-H, N-H, and O-H bond angles in methane, ammonia, and water respectively.
Interact with a visual model demonstrating how lone pair electron density occupies more angular space, pushing bonding pairs closer together.
